column4: Charts leave clues. Patterns and indicators are the tools that read those clues, and they hint at what price might do next. Notice the word hint. Nothing here is a guarantee. A pattern can fail, and an indicator can flash the wrong signal. Used with care, though, these tools stack the odds a little more in your favor. Let's meet the ones worth knowing.

Some shapes show up again and again because human behavior repeats. Look at the head and shoulders drawing on screen: three peaks, a taller head in the middle, two lower shoulders on either side, and a neckline running underneath. When price breaks below that neckline, traders read it as a possible reversal. A double top and a double bottom tell a similar story, where price tests a level twice and either gets rejected or holds. Wedges are continuation shapes, a pause before the trend picks back up. One rule ties them together: a breakout means more when volume rises with it. This drawing is illustrative, a clean textbook version of a messy real chart.

A moving average smooths the noise. It takes price over a chosen period and plots the average, so the jagged line becomes a flowing one. Watch the two smooth lines on screen. A simple moving average, the S M A, weights every period the same. An exponential moving average, the E M A, leans harder on recent prices, so it turns faster. When a shorter average crosses above a longer one, traders call it a golden cross, and read it as bullish. When the shorter one crosses below, that is a death cross, read as bearish. Same lines, opposite meaning, depending on which way they cross.

Oscillators measure momentum: how fast and how far price has moved. The most common is the R S I, the relative strength index, which runs from zero to one hundred. Above seventy is generally called overbought, and below thirty generally oversold. The stochastic works much the same way, using eighty and twenty as its markers. Here is the honest part. These are momentum meters, not crystal balls. A stock can stay overbought far longer than feels reasonable. They tell you the temperature, not the future.

Your turn. Drag the slider to set an R S I reading and watch the zone change. Slide it down toward the twenties and it turns blue for oversold. Park it in the middle and it reads a neutral green. Push it up past seventy and it glows red for overbought. Get a feel for where those edges sit. Just keep in mind what the note under the dial says: R S I is one signal, not a promise.

Now put it together. Each card on screen describes something happening on a chart. Tap a card, then drop it into bullish or bearish. A golden cross and a double bottom lean bullish. A death cross and an overbought reading lean bearish. Sort all eight and see how many you read correctly. This is exactly the kind of quick judgment you will make when a real chart is in front of you.
Five quick questions to lock it in. Take your time, and answer them to earn your points for this lesson.

Quick recap. Patterns like the head and shoulders hint at reversals, and volume helps confirm a breakout. Moving averages smooth price, and their crosses signal shifts. Oscillators like R S I read momentum, not certainty. Every one of these is a clue, never a guarantee. Next we switch from the chart to the company itself.
